verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. Same decomposition, written in Cartesian components and in the s = r²/2 chart. Three rewritings. (i) The radial operator: LeadingStress.radialDivergence k S p = √(2s)∂_s S + k S/√(2s); with r = √(2s) and ∂_r = r∂_s this is exactly (∂_r + k/r)S, and the Lean uses k = 2 on the azimuthal profile and k = 1 on the axial profile, matching the paper's 2/r and 1/r. (ii) The frame: tangentialStressForce returns AxisymmetricResidual.pack (x₁a/r) (-x₀a/r) (-z), and pack α β γ is the Cartesian vector (α,β,γ) (AxisymmetricResidual.lean:18) while e_θ = (-x₁/r, x₀/r, 0) (LocalAngularScalar.angularDirection, LocalAngularScalar.lean:20), so (x₁a/r, -x₀a/r, 0) = -a·e_θ and the third slot is -z·e_z: the two leading minus signs of the paper are reproduced. (iii) ℛ is ProblemStatement.navierStokesResidual and ℰ_B is FinalSlowBase.error = BaseResidual.baseResidual. Two things worth recording rather than scoring. First, the Lean identity is definitional: baseResidual is *defined* as navierStokesResidual - baseStressForce, so baseResidual_identity (BaseResidual.lean:1490) is proved by `unfold baseResidual; abel`. The paper's display reads the same way — ℰ_B is whatever is left over — and the mathematical content sits in the adjacent sentences (𝒯_phys supported in the annulus with leading term T; ℰ_B flat), which are stated separately (e.g. the AllJetsFlat clause of exists_final_base at FinalSlowBase.lean:681). Second, because it is definitional the Lean identity holds for every z, including on the axis r = 0 where the paper's displayed operators are not defined; Lean's total division convention absorbs this. Neither point changes what the formula says.
